_comment: DRAFT -- NOT live. Saints levels 10-12 of 23: level 10 is new (Joan of Arc -- trial, execution, 1456 posthumous retrial, 1920 canonization). Level 11 carries the old live level 3's Ignatius and level 4's Teresa of Avila/John of the Cross content forward (renumbered, re-seeded) plus new material on the Spiritual Exercises, the Discalced Carmelite reform, and the shared 1622 canonization. Level 12 carries the old live level 8's Thomas More content forward plus new material on his Lord Chancellorship, his 1535 execution, his 1935 canonization, and his 2000 patronage of statesmen. CCC 2044/2242/2731/2712/828/882, and magisterial_document citations already reviewed are reused throughout.

questions.prompt: St. Joan of Arc, a peasant girl who believed herself guided by heavenly voices, led French forces during which major conflict of the early 15th century?
choices: The Hundred Years' War
The Crusades
The Western Schism's own armed disputes
The Investiture Controversy
questions.explanation: Joan, not yet twenty, convinced the French crown to let her lead troops against English forces occupying much of France -- an astonishing role for an uneducated peasant girl in the 15th century, and one she insisted came directly from voices she believed were sent by God.
questions.hint: This long conflict between England and France was already well over a century old by Joan's time.

questions.prompt: True or False: Joan of Arc was captured, tried by an ecclesiastical court under English political influence, and burned at the stake as a heretic in 1431.
questions.explanation: True. Joan's trial was heavily shaped by English political interests eager to discredit her; she was condemned and executed at just nineteen -- a real, documented injustice this level does not soften or explain away.
questions.hint: Consider whose political interests were most served by her condemnation.

questions.prompt: What happened to Joan of Arc's original conviction roughly twenty-five years after her execution?
choices: A papal-authorized retrial formally annulled it, declaring her innocent
It was quietly forgotten with no further Church action of any kind
It was upheld again by a second, independent ecclesiastical trial
It was annulled by the French crown alone, without any Church involvement
questions.correctAnswer: A papal-authorized retrial formally annulled it, declaring her innocent
questions.explanation: In 1456, a retrial authorized by the Pope examined the original proceedings and formally declared Joan innocent, nullifying the earlier verdict -- the Church correcting an injustice carried out, in significant part, in its own name.
questions.hint: This process specifically re-examined and reversed the earlier verdict.

questions.prompt: St. Joan of Arc was canonized in the year ____, nearly five hundred years after her death, by Pope Benedict XV.
questions.explanation: Between the 1456 annulment and this 1920 canonization lies nearly half a millennium -- the Church's recognition of a person's holiness can take a genuinely long time, especially after a real historical injustice has to be untangled first.
questions.hint: This canonization comes shortly after the end of the First World War.

questions.prompt: True or False: Joan of Arc's story shows that the Church's own institutions and processes can, in a given case, be used to carry out a real injustice against someone later recognized as a saint.
questions.explanation: True, and this level does not shy away from it. Sainthood does not mean the Church's institutions are incapable of grave error in a specific case -- it means the Church, however slowly, is also capable of recognizing and formally correcting that error, as the 1456 retrial and 1920 canonization together show.
questions.hint: Consider what both the 1431 trial and the 1456 retrial, taken together, actually demonstrate.

questions.prompt: Match each fact about St. Joan of Arc to what it involves.

pairs.right: Joan leads French forces during the Hundred Years' War
Condemned and burned at the stake as a heretic
A papal-authorized retrial formally annuls her conviction

questions.explanation: Nearly five centuries separate her death from her canonization -- a real, documented arc from condemnation to correction to formal recognition, not a single simple event.
questions.hint: Read these four dates as one continuous story, not four unrelated facts.

questions.prompt: True or False: Like Catherine of Siena in the previous level, Joan of Arc held no ordained office and belonged to no religious order when she carried out the actions for which she is remembered.
questions.explanation: True. Joan, like Catherine before her, is a real case of lay sainthood -- ordinary in social standing, extraordinary in the documented consequences of her actions, continuing a pattern this topic has now shown twice in a row.
questions.hint: Recall Catherine's own state of life from the previous level.

questions.prompt: What does Joan of Arc's case add to this topic's picture of how canonization actually works, beyond what earlier levels have already shown?
choices: That the process can take an extraordinarily long time when a real historical injustice needs untangling first -- in her case, nearly five centuries
That canonization always happens within just a few short years of a candidate's own death
That the Church has never once, in the entirety of its whole very long history, recognized an error in a past judgment
That lay sainthood is entirely impossible without a formally founded religious order behind it
questions.correctAnswer: That the process can take an extraordinarily long time when a real historical injustice needs untangling first -- in her case, nearly five centuries
questions.explanation: This is new information this level adds to the topic's growing picture of canonization -- a picture the topic will return to directly, in full, several levels ahead when it covers the process itself.
questions.hint: Consider the actual span of years between Joan's death and her eventual canonization.

questions.prompt: Joan of Arc is remembered today as a patron saint of ____, alongside her broader recognition as a national heroine of France.
questions.explanation: Her sainthood and her national significance are not two separate stories -- the same documented actions that shaped a real military and political outcome are exactly what the Church later recognized as holiness lived out in extraordinary circumstances.
questions.hint: The country whose forces she led, and which venerates her as both saint and national heroine.

questions.prompt: Given Joan's story on the eve of the Reformation, what does the next level in this topic turn to?
choices: A new generation of saints responding directly to the Reformation itself -- Ignatius of Loyola, Teresa of Ávila, and John of the Cross
A complete and exhaustive repeat of Joan's own story, with no new figures introduced at all
A jump backward to the apostolic era, which this topic has already fully covered many levels earlier
A subject entirely and completely unrelated to sainthood or to the historical periods this topic has covered
questions.correctAnswer: A new generation of saints responding directly to the Reformation itself -- Ignatius of Loyola, Teresa of Ávila, and John of the Cross
questions.explanation: Joan's death in 1431 comes barely a century before Luther's own 1517 protest -- the next level turns to the saints the Catholic Reformation itself produced in direct response to that crisis, already covered from Church History's own angle.
questions.hint: This is exactly what the next level in this topic covers.

questions.prompt: St. Ignatius of Loyola founded the Society of Jesus, approved by Pope Paul III in 1540; its members are commonly known as ____.
questions.explanation: Ignatius's new order emphasized rigorous formation, missionary flexibility, and direct obedience to the Pope -- becoming one of the most influential religious orders in the Church's history, and a direct response to the Reformation crisis Church History covers independently.
questions.hint: This nickname for the Society of Jesus is still used worldwide today.

questions.prompt: St. Teresa of Ávila's most famous mystical work, describing the soul's journey toward God through seven dwelling places, is called what?
choices: The Interior Castle
The Ascent of Mount Carmel
The Dialogue
The Cloud of Unknowing
questions.explanation: Teresa pictured the soul as a castle of many rooms, with God dwelling at its very center -- one of the most influential works of Christian mysticism, part of why Paul VI declared her a Doctor of the Church in 1970.
questions.hint: She pictured the soul itself as a great fortress with many rooms.

citations.reference: Paul VI, declaring St. Teresa of Ávila a Doctor of the Church (1970)

questions.prompt: True or False: St. John of the Cross, a close collaborator of St. Teresa of Ávila in reforming the Carmelite order, wrote of the soul's purification in a work called 'The Dark Night of the Soul.'
questions.explanation: John of the Cross described the painful but purifying experience of feeling God's absence on the way to deeper union with him -- teaching so influential that Pius XI declared him a Doctor of the Church in 1926.
questions.hint: The title of his most famous work describes a period of spiritual darkness.

citations.reference: Pius XI, declaring St. John of the Cross a Doctor of the Church (1926)

questions.prompt: True or False: St. John of the Cross's 'dark night' describes a purification God brings about, not a sign of the soul's failure or abandonment.
questions.explanation: True. The darkness is God's own action, withdrawing felt consolation so the soul's attachment shifts from spiritual gifts to God himself -- not evidence that something has gone wrong.
questions.hint: Ask whose action, according to John, the darkness actually is.

questions.prompt: Ignatius of Loyola composed a structured, month-long program of prayer and self-examination that remains central to Jesuit formation and retreats today. What is it called?
choices: The Spiritual Exercises
The Rule of St. Ignatius
The Way of Perfection
The Imitation of Christ
questions.explanation: Ignatius developed the Exercises out of his own dramatic conversion, recovering from a battlefield wound -- a structured path meant to help a person discern God's will and reorder their whole life around it.
questions.hint: This work is literally named for the discipline of prayer it walks a person through.

questions.prompt: True or False: Teresa of Ávila and John of the Cross together reformed the Carmelite order, founding what became known as the Discalced (barefoot) Carmelites.
questions.explanation: True. Both sought a return to the order's original, stricter observance -- a reform that, like Dominic's own founding several levels earlier, answered a real crisis of discipline and fervor within religious life itself.
questions.hint: This reform's name describes the simple, unshod sandals the reformed friars and nuns wore.

questions.prompt: Match each Counter-Reformation saint to what makes them one of this level's figures.

pairs.right: Founded the Jesuits and wrote the Spiritual Exercises
Wrote The Interior Castle and reformed the Carmelites
Wrote The Dark Night of the Soul, reformed alongside Teresa
The stricter reform Teresa and John founded together

questions.explanation: All three figures respond, in their own distinct way, to the same 16th-century moment Church History covers as the Catholic Reformation -- renewal from within, not merely reaction against the Reformation outside.
questions.hint: Three rows name individual founders; one names the reform two of them founded together.

questions.prompt: In 1622, four major figures of the Catholic Reformation were canonized together on the same day. Ignatius of Loyola and Teresa of Ávila were two; who else was included?
choices: St. Francis Xavier and St. Philip Neri
St. Dominic and St. Clare of Assisi
St. Benedict and St. Scholastica
St. Catherine of Siena and St. Joan of Arc
questions.correctAnswer: St. Francis Xavier and St. Philip Neri
questions.explanation: This shared canonization day is itself a striking sign of how concentrated real holiness was in this single generation's response to the Reformation crisis -- four major figures, recognized together, rather than spread across separate ceremonies decades apart.
questions.hint: One of these two was Ignatius's own missionary companion, already covered in Church History's treatment of the missions.

citations.quote: By canonizing some of the faithful... the Church recognizes the power of the Spirit of holiness within her and sustains the hope of believers by proposing the saints to them as models and intercessors.

questions.prompt: A phrase closely associated with Ignatian spirituality describes seeking and recognizing God's presence in every ordinary circumstance of daily life: finding God in all ____.
questions.explanation: This principle -- that holiness is not confined to explicitly religious moments but can be found in any faithfully lived circumstance -- has shaped Jesuit spirituality, education, and mission for nearly five centuries since Ignatius's own death.
questions.hint: The phrase insists God can be found in every ordinary circumstance, not only in explicitly religious moments.

questions.prompt: Given this level's picture of renewal from within the Church itself, what does the next level in this topic turn to?
choices: St. Thomas More, a layman martyred in England for refusing to compromise his faith under Henry VIII
A complete repeat of this same level's material about the Counter-Reformation saints
A jump backward to Joan of Arc's own era, already fully covered
A subject entirely unrelated to the Reformation era or to sainthood of any kind
questions.correctAnswer: St. Thomas More, a layman martyred in England for refusing to compromise his faith under Henry VIII
questions.explanation: The next level turns from renewal within Catholic Europe to a very different, harder story unfolding at the very same time in England -- a return to martyrdom, the pattern this topic opened with many levels ago, now playing out under a new set of political pressures.
questions.hint: This is exactly what the next level in this topic covers.

questions.prompt: St. Thomas More refused to sign the Act of Succession's oath acknowledging Henry VIII as Supreme Head of the Church in England. What specific doctrinal stake was More resisting?
choices: A rejection of papal primacy and the unity of the Church under the Roman See
A narrow dispute over the exact number of sacraments the Church recognizes
A disagreement concerning the correct date for celebrating Easter
An objection specifically to the continued use of Latin in the liturgy
questions.correctAnswer: A rejection of papal primacy and the unity of the Church under the Roman See
questions.explanation: Henry VIII's Act of Supremacy asserted royal headship over the Church in England in place of the Pope, a direct rejection of papal primacy. More's refusal to sign, which cost him his life in 1535, was a witness to the unity of the Church under Peter's successor.
questions.hint: This is fundamentally a dispute about who has ultimate authority over the Church, not a liturgical or sacramental dispute.

citations.quote: The Pope, Bishop of Rome and Peter's successor, 'is the perpetual and visible source and foundation of the unity both of the bishops and of the whole company of the faithful.'

questions.prompt: What was St. Thomas More's stated ground for refusing the oath, according to his own account?
choices: The oath required acknowledging a spiritual supremacy he believed belonged to the Pope alone, which he could not affirm
He objected only to the specific tax implications contained within the Act itself
He had, in fact, supported Henry's annulment but opposed only the specific succession terms themselves
His refusal concerned, in the end, a purely personal grievance he held against the king
questions.correctAnswer: The oath required acknowledging a spiritual supremacy he believed belonged to the Pope alone, which he could not affirm
questions.explanation: More's own account frames this as a matter of conscience about a specific claim -- royal supremacy over the Church -- not a general political grievance, which is why his martyrdom is remembered as a witness to conscience formed by truth over political convenience.
questions.hint: Ask what specific claim, not a general political complaint, the oath actually required affirming.

questions.prompt: True or False: Before his conflict with Henry VIII, Thomas More held the powerful civil office of Lord Chancellor of England.
questions.explanation: True. More was one of the King's own most trusted advisors before their break -- his sainthood is not the story of a marginal outsider but of a man at the very center of political power who chose conscience over that power when the two finally came into direct conflict.
questions.hint: Consider how close to the center of royal power More actually stood before his refusal.

questions.prompt: More is often remembered for a final statement, declaring himself the King's good servant, but ____ first.
questions.explanation: This line captures exactly the distinction his whole conflict turned on -- real, ordinary loyalty to the crown, but never loyalty that could override a deeper obligation to God and conscience.
questions.hint: The phrase names the one authority More placed even above the king himself.

questions.prompt: True or False: Thomas More was executed by beheading in 1535 after his conviction.
questions.explanation: True. More was tried, convicted largely on the basis of disputed testimony, and beheaded in July 1535 -- a swift and brutal end for a man who had spent his career as one of England's most respected scholars and statesmen.
questions.hint: Consider what year, and what method, his execution actually took.

questions.prompt: Match each fact about St. Thomas More to what it involves.

pairs.right: The powerful civil office More held before his refusal
Required acknowledging Henry VIII's supremacy over the Church

pairs.left: "The King's good servant, but God's first"
pairs.right: More's own statement of where his ultimate loyalty lay
The year of More's execution by beheading

questions.explanation: This level's arc runs from real political power to real, costly refusal -- a martyrdom that happens in the full public view of England's own government, not in secret or on the margins.
questions.hint: Follow More's own arc: office held, oath refused, reason stated, consequence faced.

questions.prompt: In what year was St. Thomas More formally canonized, four hundred years after his execution?
questions.explanation: Pope Pius XI canonized More on the exact four-hundredth anniversary of his death -- a deliberate, symbolic timing recognizing his martyrdom as still speaking directly to the Church's own concerns four centuries later.
questions.hint: This date is exactly four centuries after his 1535 execution.

questions.prompt: True or False: In the year 2000, Pope John Paul II declared St. Thomas More the patron saint of statesmen and politicians.
questions.explanation: True. This declaration ties More's specific witness -- holding real political power without letting it override conscience -- directly to the vocation of anyone exercising public office today.
questions.hint: This declaration ties his specific witness directly to a vocation exercised today.

questions.prompt: What does More's martyrdom add to this topic's growing picture of sainthood, compared to the Counter-Reformation saints covered in the previous level?
choices: Real, costly witness under direct political pressure from one's own government, not renewal chosen from within the Church
Nothing new -- his path is functionally identical to Ignatius's founding of the Jesuits
Proof that sainthood was impossible for anyone holding real political power
A return to the exact same martyrdom pattern already covered in level 4's Roman martyrs, with no real difference
questions.correctAnswer: Real, costly witness under direct political pressure from one's own government, not renewal chosen from within the Church
questions.explanation: This level's saint is not a founder or reformer choosing renewal -- he is a layman whose own government demanded he compromise his conscience, and who refused at the cost of his life, closer in shape to level 4's ancient martyrs than to level 11's reformers, but under an entirely different set of political circumstances.
questions.hint: Compare the pressure More faced -- from his own government -- to what Ignatius, Teresa, and John of the Cross faced in the previous level.

questions.prompt: Given More's witness at the height of political power, what does the next level in this topic turn to?
choices: Missionary saints of the age of exploration -- Francis Xavier, carrying the Gospel across a rapidly widening world
A complete repeat of this same level's material about Thomas More
A jump backward to Joan of Arc's own era, already fully covered
A subject entirely unrelated to sainthood or to the historical period this topic has reached
questions.correctAnswer: Missionary saints of the age of exploration -- Francis Xavier, carrying the Gospel across a rapidly widening world
questions.explanation: The next level moves outward from Europe's own internal struggles to the missionary frontier this same century opened -- already covered from Church History's own angle, and now returned to from the angle of the individual saint himself.
questions.hint: This is exactly what the next level in this topic covers.

citations.quote: By canonizing some of the faithful... the Church recognizes the power of the Spirit of holiness within her and sustains the hope of believers by proposing the saints to them as models and intercessors.
